prompt: Which Ubuntu package gives you the compiler `javac` as well as the launcher?
hint: The kit for writing Java, not only for running it.

choices.text: `openjdk-25-jdk`
choices.why: Right. The JDK carries `javac`, `java` and tools like `javap`.

choices.text: `java-common`, which every Java package depends on
choices.why: It holds shared configuration and no compiler.

choices.text: `openjdk-25-jre`
choices.why: That is the runtime alone: it runs Java and cannot compile it.

choices.text: `maven`
choices.why: Maven builds projects and needs a JDK underneath it.

prompt: `mvn -B -v` prints `Java version: 25.0.4.1` on its third line. What does that line tell you?
hint: Maven is itself a Java program.

choices.text: The newest Java that Maven supports
choices.why: It reports what it found, not a limit.

choices.text: The Java that Maven itself found and runs on
choices.why: Right. Maven runs on whichever Java it finds, which is why this is the line to read first.

choices.text: The version of Maven
choices.why: That is the first line, `Apache Maven 3.8.7`.

choices.text: The Java your programs will be compiled for, whatever the project says
choices.why: The project's own settings decide the target; this line is the Java Maven runs on.

prompt: After `java Hello.java` printed its line, `ls` showed only `Hello.java`. Why is there no `Hello.class`?

choices.text: Java 25 interprets source code without compiling it
choices.why: It does compile, to bytecode, only not to a file.

choices.text: It was compiled in memory, not to a file
choices.why: Right. Source-file mode compiles in memory and runs the result.

choices.text: The class file went into `~/.m2`
choices.why: That is Maven's local repository of libraries.

choices.text: `java` deleted it as soon as the program had finished
choices.why: Nothing was written to delete.

prompt: A runtime says `class file version 69.0` and `only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0`. What happened?

choices.text: The class file was damaged when copied
choices.why: A damaged file fails with a different error, about its format.

choices.text: Maven was given the wrong `JAVA_HOME`
choices.why: Maven was not involved; this is `java` itself refusing a class.

choices.text: Code compiled by Java 21 was run by Java 25
choices.why: That direction works: newer runtimes read older class files.

choices.text: Code compiled by Java 25 was run by a Java 21 runtime
choices.why: Right. A runtime refuses class files newer than itself.

prompt: `mvn -B -v` reports Java 21 although `java -version` says 25. Where does Maven get its Java from?
hint: A variable a guide told you to put in `~/.bashrc`.

choices.text: From the newest JDK in `/usr/lib/jvm`
choices.why: Maven does not search that folder by version.

choices.text: From `JAVA_HOME`, when it is set
choices.why: Right. When `JAVA_HOME` is set, Maven uses that Java rather than the one on the `PATH`.

choices.text: From the `pom.xml` of the project
choices.why: `mvn -v` was run outside any project.

choices.text: From the Java it was built with, years ago
choices.why: It runs on the Java it finds now.

prompt: The compiler reports three errors, the first `illegal character: '\u201c'`. What should you do first?
hint: The other two may be consequences.

choices.text: Fix the last error, which is the one closest to the cause
choices.why: Compilers report in order; the first is closest to the cause.

choices.text: Install a newer JDK that accepts typographic quotes
choices.why: No Java accepts them as string delimiters.

choices.text: Fix the first one, retyping the quotes, and compile again
choices.why: Right. `not a statement` was only a consequence of the rejected quotes.

choices.text: Fix all three before compiling again
choices.why: The third disappears with the first; chasing it wastes time.

prompt: Compiling `BeforeLambdas.java` produced `BeforeLambdas$1.class`. Which part of the program is that file?
hint: One of the two comparators became a class of its own.

choices.text: The lambda
choices.why: The lambda's body became the method `lambda$main$0` inside `BeforeLambdas`.

choices.text: A copy of `List` made for the second sort
choices.why: Lists are objects at run time, not classes the compiler writes.

choices.text: The `main` method
choices.why: `main` is inside `BeforeLambdas.class`.

choices.text: The anonymous `Comparator` class from the first sort
choices.why: Right. An anonymous class is a class, and gets a file.

prompt: `javap -c` showed three `invokedynamic` instructions in `BeforeLambdas`, and the program has one lambda. Where do the other two come from?
hint: Look at what they say after `InvokeDynamic`.

choices.text: From the anonymous class, which also uses `invokedynamic`
choices.why: The anonymous class is created with `new`, from its own class file.

choices.text: From the two calls to `sort`
choices.why: A method call on an object is `invokeinterface` or `invokevirtual`.

choices.text: From `List.of`, which builds its list lazily
choices.why: `List.of` is an ordinary static method call.

choices.text: From the two string concatenations with `+`
choices.why: Right: `makeConcatWithConstants`. Since Java 9 the compiler joins strings with `invokedynamic` too.

prompt: `Dune` and `Emma` have the same length. After the sort they are still in the order they were given. Why?

choices.text: `List.sort` is stable
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: By chance; another run may swap them
choices.why: Stability is guaranteed, not luck.

choices.text: Strings of equal length are never compared
choices.why: They are compared, and the comparator answers 0.

choices.text: The comparator breaks ties between equal lengths in alphabetical order
choices.why: It compares lengths and nothing else.

prompt: Match each lambda with the rule its form illustrates.

pairs.right: One parameter may drop its brackets
Written types go on every parameter

right_distractors: A lambda must declare its return type

prompt: `var twice = (Integer x) -> x * 2;` does not compile. Why?
hint: Each side waits for the other to give it a type.

choices.text: Parameter types are forbidden inside a lambda's brackets
choices.why: They are allowed; `Shapes.java` writes them.

choices.text: `Integer` cannot be multiplied
choices.why: It is unboxed to `int` for the multiplication.

choices.text: `var` gives the lambda no target type
choices.why: Right: `lambda expression needs an explicit target-type`.

choices.text: `var` cannot hold an object
choices.why: `var` holds any object whose type the right-hand side states.

prompt: The type a lambda takes from the variable or parameter it is written for is called its ___ type.
`greeter` has returned, and the lambda it built still prints its local `greeting`. How?

choices.text: The lambda calls `greeter` again to get it
choices.why: `greeter` runs once.

choices.text: `greeting` is a field of `Capture`
choices.why: It is declared inside `greeter`; `shop` is the field.

choices.text: The local variable lives on until the program ends
choices.why: Locals end with their method; the lambda kept its own copy.

choices.text: The lambda keeps a copy of the value
choices.why: Right, and that copy is why the variable must not change.

prompt: Which of these can a lambda written inside an instance method read? Choose all that apply.
hint: The rule covers locals and nothing else.

choices.text: A local the lambda increments
choices.why: No: `Counter.java`'s error.

choices.text: A local assigned twice before the lambda
choices.why: No. `Reassigned.java` showed that it is refused.

choices.text: A field of the object that is reassigned later
choices.why: Yes. Fields are read through `this`, which never changes.

choices.text: A local assigned once and never again
choices.why: Yes: effectively final.

choices.text: The method's own parameter, never reassigned
choices.why: Yes, like `visitor` in `greeter`.

prompt: In `WhoIsThis.show()`, a lambda prints `this`. Which object is that?
hint: A lambda is not a class.

choices.text: The lambda object itself
choices.why: That is what an anonymous class's `this` would be.

choices.text: The `Runnable` interface
choices.why: `this` is always an object, never an interface.

choices.text: None: `this` is a compile error in a lambda
choices.why: It compiles and means the enclosing object.

choices.text: The one `show()` was called on
choices.why: Right: `lambda sees: the WhoIsThis object`.

prompt: Put the life of the lambda in `again.sort((a, b) -> ...)` in order.
hint: From the compiler to the last comparison.
items: `javac` puts the body in a private method, `lambda$main$0`
`invokedynamic` asks the JVM to build a `Comparator` around it
`sort` calls `compare`, which runs the body, once per comparison

prompt: Counting in a `forEach` with `n++` on a local is refused. What does section 06 recommend instead?
hint: The best counter is one nobody has to change.

choices.text: Let a stream do it, with lesson 7's `count()`
choices.why: Right. The lesson points at lesson 7 for this.

choices.text: Write `var n = 0` so the compiler infers the type
choices.why: `var` changes nothing about effectively final.

choices.text: Move `n` into a field of the object and increment it there
choices.why: It compiles, and is the shared mutable state lessons 11 to 14 warn about.

choices.text: Declare `n` as `final`
choices.why: Then `count++` is refused for a second reason.
